units.la: {Q}uanquam summam Tuam Bene-volentiam, pari conjunctione prudentiæ firma-tam, sæpius mihi animadvertere licuerit, supe-rioribus tamen literis ad me datis, ita illa emi-nuit, ut non animorum modo copula, & optima cognitione Tua circa propositam materiam per-amanter frui, sed uno quasi ore corporeque Te-cum esse viderer. Placuerunt mihi, quæ nuperrimis meis adde-re voluisti argumenta omnimodo, & accuratè Te disseruisse, & conquisitis rationibus rem præsentis Pacis nostræ Te attigisse, fateor:
units.tr: Although I have often had occasion to notice your great goodwill, joined with an equal measure of prudence, your earlier letter to me showed it so clearly that I seemed not only to enjoy the bond of our minds and your excellent knowledge of the matter in hand, very lovingly, but to be with you as if we shared one mouth and one body. I admit that I was pleased with the arguments you wished to add to my most recent letter, and that you have discussed them thoroughly and touched on the present peace between us with carefully gathered reasons.

units.la: Cùm enim DEI & fatorum voluntate bellum inter tam potentes Accolas Orbis nostri Romano-Germanici novissimè concitatum fuerit celerrime, & sicut bellicosum populum decet, sub initium illi totis viribus incumberent concertantes, eo peracto, quam celerrime illud quoque solutum fuisse, prudentis consilii erat.
units.tr: Since by the will of God and of fate the war that recently arose between such powerful neighbours of our Roman-German world was fought out with great speed, and, as is fitting for a warlike people, they struggled at the outset with all their strength, it was the mark of a prudent plan that, once that was over, it should also be settled as quickly as possible.

units.la: Id quod olim jam observasse Lacedæmones Thucydides meminit: hi enim de concilianda pace acturi, & eo fine ad Athenienses missi, inter cætera, quæ Senatui populoque proponebant, & hæc sub finem orationis suæ, notanter dixerant: Dum belli eventus adhuc anceps est: Vos quidem cum gloria, nostraque Amicitiæ accessione, & nos antequam dedecus nobis accidat, cum mediocri tolera-bilique jactura, in gratiam redeamus.
units.tr: Thucydides records that the Lacedaemonians had already observed this. When they came to Athens to arrange peace, and for that purpose, among other things they proposed to the Senate and people, they said pointedly at the end of their speech: While the outcome of the war is still doubtful, you may return to favour with us with glory and the addition of our friendship, and we before disgrace comes upon us, with a moderate and bearable loss.

units.la: Hoc Lacedæmoniorum consilium & suo ævo sequutos esse, Anglos, cum de finiendo quod cum Scotis ipsis intercesserat bello, inter illos convenisset, insignis ille rerum Scoticarum Historicus, Buchananus nobis commemorat. Belli casus dubios esse, differebant Angli, exitum quoque incertum, Virorum itaque prudentium non esse, quæ ante oculos esset utilitatem negligere, & certo periculo in spem in-certam incumbere.
units.tr: That the English followed this same counsel in their own age, when they agreed with the Scots to end the war between them, the distinguished historian of Scottish affairs, Buchanan, tells us. The English argued: The chances of war are uncertain, and its outcome is also unclear. It is not the mark of prudent men to neglect the advantage that lies before their eyes and to rush into an uncertain hope with a certain danger.

units.la: Quis non Turcarum insolentiam indignitatemq; armorum suorum, proterviam pariter potentiæ Turcicæ novit? at quoties novimus & illos ipsos remisisse suos Spiritus. Anno Christi 1444. ingenti clade ad Varnam oppidum, Regem Hungariæ Uladislaum prostraverant, & penes eos erat Hungariam hac clade maximè percussam, omnino subjugare: Amurathes autem, qui de hac victoria ob tot & tantos e suis quoque desideratos, non adeò exultare poterat, ita ut domum reversus sæpius exclamasse dicatur: Se nolle hoc modo sæpius vincere, cum elisas proprias suas post hoc prælium cerneret vires, præter opinionem omnium per aliquod tempus otium & quietem Hungariæ concessit & copias suas domum remisit. Anno Christi 1570. Insula Cyprus sub Mustaphæ & Priuli Selimi II. Prætorum, signis, jugum recepit Ottomanni-cum, Sultano eapropter superbissimè triumphante, cum autem subsequente anno, sub Ducibus Johanne Austriaco & Sebastiano Veneri, Venetorum postea Duce, nec non sub auspiciis M. Antonini Columnæ ad Insulas Echinadas, ad internecionem usq; profligati essent Barbari, amissa tota quam adduxerant 250. navigiorum classe, contenti quod Cyprum Insulam non ita pridem Christianis ereptam, sartam tectam conservassent, subito cum Venetis, contectis vulneribus suis, pacem inierunt.
units.tr: Who does not know the arrogance of the Turks, the reckless pride of their arms, and the insolence of Turkish power? Yet how often have we seen even these men relax their spirit? In the year of Christ 1444 they routed King Ladislaus of Hungary with a great slaughter at the town of Varna, and it was in their power to subdue Hungary utterly, which had been struck hardest by this disaster. But Murad, who could not rejoice much in this victory, since so many and such great men of his own side had been lost, is said to have often exclaimed on returning home that he did not wish to win in this way again. Seeing that his own strength was worn down after this battle, he unexpectedly, against everyone's expectation, granted Hungary some time of rest and quiet and sent his forces home. In the year of Christ 1570 the island of Cyprus, under the commanders Mustapha and Priuli, the Venetian governors, surrendered to the Ottoman yoke, and the Sultan triumphed proudly for that reason. But in the following year, under the leaders John of Austria and Sebastian Venier, later doge of the Venetians, and under the auspices of Marcantonio Colonna, at the Echinades islands the barbarians were routed to utter destruction, and the whole fleet of 250 ships they had brought was lost. Content to have kept Cyprus, an island snatched from the Christians not long before, safe and sound, they suddenly made peace with the Venetians, their wounds still covered.

units.la: Longum esset illas, quas Leonhardus Aretinus nobis exposuit hic referre consultationes, quondam in Senatu Veneto habitas, cum Mastini della Scala, Italorum Tyranni Oratores, de Pace Italiæ danda coram Senatu agerent: Pergrave tum temporis quoque omnibus belli sociis videbatur, Venetos ad Pacem inclinare, ast illis, hoc si bellum continuandum foret, præ cæteris sociis arduum & difficile sibi futurum, testantibus, tot sumptibus jam defessis, & nulla æquitate id ipsis imponi posse docentibus, missi primum ad Venetos Sociorum Legati, ut maximè pacem hanc improbarent & dissuadere conarentur; cum nihil proficer posse cernerent, justi sunt, quoad fieri poterat, augeri conditiones contra Mastinum; tandem in sententia persistentibus Venetis, oblatam Pacem & ipsi acceptare in mandatis habebant: & ita non quid concupiscant sociorum animi, sed quid fas & jura & propria suaderet charitas, Rempublicam hoc in negotio spectasse, Venetorum Dux pro solio, Legatis respondebat. Laudatur ab Aretino hoc consilium: quidni in simili fere casu, laudandum quoq; erit Invictissimi Cæsaris nostri consilium, cum quicquid ex æquitate & justitia & amore boni publici faciendum erat, licet non ita ex dignitate Reipublicæ aliquibus fieri videatur, nihilominus faciendum esse judicaverit, ut bellum & calamitas evidetur; quod Atheniensium aliquando consilium fuisse, annotavit noster Thucydides. Et quamvis sint nonnulli, ut in Tuis monuisti, qui cum magno illo eruditi nominis Italo, Fabio Albergato, Pacem eam haud certe Pacem dicant, quæ non omnem exfundat controversiam, cum morbum nemo curasse prædicandus sit, nisi radicem morbi extinxerit, nec corpus sanum vocari possit, si timenda sit morbi reversio, nec liberatum ægrotum putemus, si qualitas morbi perseveret: cum autem e contra sint quidam morborum languores, qui gravitate sua intrinseca medicinam respuunt, & radicitus depelli non possunt, juxta illud Poëtæ:
units.tr: It would be too long to set out here the deliberations that Leonardo Aretino describes for us, once held in the Venetian Senate, when the envoys of Mastino della Scala, tyrant of the Italians, pleaded in the Senate for giving peace to Italy. At that time it also seemed very grievous to all the allies in the war that the Venetians were inclined to peace. But the envoys of the allies, who said that if the war were to be continued it would be harder and more difficult for them than for the other allies, since they were already worn out by such expenses and could show that no fairness could be imposed on them, were sent first to the Venetians to oppose and dissuade them from this peace as strongly as possible. When they saw that nothing could be gained, they were ordered to increase the terms against Mastino as far as possible. Finally, since the Venetians persisted in their view, the envoys had instructions to accept the peace offered as well. The Doge of Venice, speaking from his throne, told the envoys that the Republic in this matter had looked not to what the allies' desires craved, but to what right, justice and proper charity advised. Aretino praises this counsel. Why should we not likewise praise the counsel of our most invincible Emperor in a case that is nearly similar, since he judged that whatever ought to be done in accordance with fairness, justice and love of the common good had to be done, even though it may seem to some not in keeping with the dignity of the Republic, so that the war and its calamity might end? Our Thucydides noted that this was once the counsel of the Athenians. And although there are some, as you pointed out in your letter, who, with that great Italian scholar Fabio Albergati, say that this is certainly not a peace which does not remove all controversy, since no one can be said to have cured a disease unless he has destroyed its root, nor can a body be called sound if the return of the disease is to be feared, nor can we think the patient freed if the nature of the disease persists. Yet on the other hand there are some weaknesses of diseases which by their inherent severity reject medicine and cannot be driven out root and branch, according to the saying of the poet:

units.la: Curando fieri quædam majora videmus vulnera, quæ melius non tetigisse fuit:
units.tr: In curing, we see some wounds become greater, which it would have been better not to touch.

units.la: Eam quoque honestam & gloriosam Pacem pronunciabimus, quæ gaudent voluntarii, quo titulo pacisicentes Magnates nostros, omni jure insignire hodie possumus, quæ nihil habet insidiarum, quæ non est pactio servitutis, & quæ nomine Pacis nullas potest se trahit clandestinas subversiones, hanc merito & nos ratam habeamus, cum ab EO, quem probamus omnes, nempe à Cæsare nostro, ita judicatum esse videamus: Liceat Ciceronis verba lib. I. de natura Deorum, hic quoque mea facere?
units.tr: We shall also pronounce that peace honourable and glorious which pleases those who make it willingly, a title by which we can today fully honour our peacemaking magnates, which has no treachery, which is not a bargain for slavery, and which under the name of peace does not drag along any secret subversions. We should rightly hold this peace valid too, since we see it has been so judged by him whom all of us approve, namely our Emperor. May I make Cicero's words from the first book of On the Nature of the Gods my own here too?

units.la: Hæc etiam aliquando mens erat laudatissimæ Reginæ Isabellæ, Ferdinandi Catholici Conjugis, cum Mendoza Cardinalis, Hispanus, de pace Hispano-Lusitana cum illa agere inciperet:
units.tr: This also was once the mind of the most praiseworthy Queen Isabella, wife of Ferdinand the Catholic, when the Spanish Cardinal Mendoza began to negotiate with her a peace between Spain and Portugal.

units.la: Etsi respondebat Regina Cardinali, omnia sub dubia etiamnum belli fortuna pendeant, se tamen non permissuram aliquam servitutem, passuram autem, ut voluntariam, ut pro redimenda Hispanici Orbis tranquillitate dependeretur Lusitano tantum auri, quantum bonis Viris, utriusque partis aestimatoribus visum erit; de quo nobis egregia, sollertissimus ille rerum Hispanicarum Historiographus, Ælius Antoninus Nebrissensis, enarrat.
units.tr: The Queen answered the Cardinal that, while all things still hang on the uncertain fortune of war, she would not permit any slavery, but would allow it to be given, as a voluntary act, to the Portuguese for the sake of securing the tranquillity of the Spanish world, as much gold as good men, appraisers of both sides, should judge fitting. Ælius Antonius Nebrissensis, that most skilled historian of Spanish affairs, relates this matter to us in an excellent way.

units.la: Imo vel unicum hoc procul ab omni affectu perpendamus, quod nobis Romanus ille Historicus Livius proponit: hoc quasi a natura comparatum esse, ut nisi prius nostra defenderimus, aliena oppugnatum non eamus, adeoque providendum sit, ut nostris prius decedat timor, quam aliis inferatur. Quod Philippum II. Viscontium, Johannis Galeatii filium, cum ex obitu fratris sui, universae Lombardiae Imperium adeptus esset, eamque ob rem magnis conatibus se non imparem putaret, fecisse, Machiavellus refert: Ad implenda igitur sua desideria accedenti, visum erat, inquit Historicus, quicquid turbidi inter ipsum & Florentinos accolas tum temporis restabat, ante omnia amovere. Eduardus III. Anglorum Rex, cum Anno Christi 1342. Scotorum indignationem vindicare vellet, quamvis cum Philippo VI. Galliarum Rege, maximo detentus esset bello, subito Tornaci in Triennium cum Eo inducias nexit, ut modo eo melius rebus Scoticis vacare posset: Id quod & Richardum II. Anglum agitasse, supra citatus Buchananus commemorat. Carolus Burgundus ut suo aevo deprimeret Lotharingum, & paulo post contra Helvetios bellum pararet, quod ipsum comitatu Feretano spoliassent, cum tantum in illos exercitium instruxisset, quantum aetas illa nondum viderat, ita ut Helvetii tum temporibus instantem Patriae suae lugubrem Statum complorantes, illum quasi deserere viderentur, & vim deprecantes, Burgundo per Legatos suos dici curarent: Pluris valere calcaria Equitum Burgundiae Ducis, quam totum Patriae suae solum, ut a latere Ludovicum XI. Gallum, Amicum haberet, nullas Pacis conditiones ipsi oblatas respuit: tulit aequo animo Connestablii Franciae, quem alii Sancti Pauli Comitem nominabant, supplicium, qui ad Carolum Burgundum supplex se receperat, Eumque postea postulanti Ludovico tradiderat, hunc per Legatos suos inter manus Ludovici hærentem, frustra postea iaivum[?] cupiebat, nam Ludovicus statim ab Eo capitis pœnam exegerat: & ita nihil omnino quamvis indignum erat, reliquit Burgundus, ut Ludovicum Gallum sibi conciliaret, quo melius & accin-ctius bello Helvetico incumbere posset, de quo plura nobis tradi-dit Cominæus. Pariter ut integro & infracto bello suam multis injuriis, ut rebatur, à Johanne Friderico Saxone, & Philippo Landgravio Hassiæ jactatam aliquoties atque exagitatam æquitatem vindicaret Carolus V. Anno Christo 1543. una cum fratre suo Ferdinando I. cum Solymanno ad certum & definitum tempus Pacem pepigit. Ipsus dicti Solymanni Filius, Amurathes III. ut Tartarorum Præcopitarum sedes in provinciam Turcicam eo facilius redigeret, Anno Christi 1584. cum Rudolpho II. Imperatore, ad novem quoque annos prorogavit inducias.
units.tr: Indeed, let us weigh this single point, free from all feeling, which the Roman historian Livy sets before us: it is, as it were, implanted by nature that we do not go out to attack others' property unless we have first defended our own, and so care must be taken that our own fear is removed before it is inflicted on others. Machiavelli reports that Philip II Visconti, son of Giangaleazzo, did this. When, on the death of his brother, he obtained the rule of all Lombardy and, for that reason, thought himself not unequal to great undertakings, then, as the historian says, to fulfil his desires as he approached, he thought it best to remove first of all whatever disturbance remained between himself and the Florentines, his neighbours, at that time. When Edward III, King of the English, in the year of Christ 1342 wanted to avenge the indignation of the Scots, although he was held in a great war with Philip VI, King of the French, he suddenly made a truce with him at Tournai for three years, so that he might attend to Scottish affairs the better for it. Buchanan, cited above, records that Richard II of England also planned this. Charles the Bold of Burgundy, in order to crush the Lorrainer in his own time, and soon after to prepare war against the Swiss, who had stripped him of the county of Ferrette, having assembled against them an army greater than that age had yet seen, so that the Swiss, lamenting the grievous state of their country under the threat of the moment, seemed to abandon it and, deprecating violence, arranged for word to be sent to Burgundy through their envoys: that the spurs of the Duke of Burgundy's horsemen were worth more than their whole native soil. He wished to have Louis XI of France as his friend at his side, and rejected all peace terms offered to him. He bore with equanimity the execution of the Constable of France, whom others called the Count of Saint-Pol, who had taken refuge as a suppliant with Charles of Burgundy and had handed him over when Louis demanded him. Afterwards the Constable, still in Louis' hands, vainly sought to act through his envoys, for Louis at once exacted the penalty of death from him. And so Burgundy left nothing whatever undone, however shameful, in order to win Louis of France to himself, so that he could attack the Swiss war better and more ready. Commines has given us more on this. Likewise, so that with the war still whole and unbroken he might avenge his fairness, which he thought had been often wounded and assailed by many injuries from John Frederick of Saxony and Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, Charles V in the year of Christ 1543 made peace with Suleiman for a fixed and defined time, together with his brother Ferdinand I. Suleiman's son, Murad III, in order to bring the seat of the Tartar Crimean Khans more easily under Turkish province, extended the truce with Rudolf II, Emperor, for nine years, in the year of Christ 1584.

units.la: Ut igitur gloriosissimus Cæsar noster, Hungarorum Rebel-lium licentiam impune quasi hactenus grassantem, tandem aliquando promptius refrænare posset, & conatus eorum ex imo reprimeret, ille etiam sub nuperrimis Pacis tractatibus res æmulorum suorum quovis modo à se amoliri prudentissime adnisus est. Et placet omnino sub hisce rerum nostrarum articulis & bel-li exagitationibus, quibus obruebamur undique, Pauli Jovii judi-cium hic adferre, quod de Tremollio Gallo protulit, cum ille tempore Ludovici XII. Gallliarum Regis Anno 1513. ad Divo-nium cum Helvetiis aliquas Pacis compositiones ex arena quasi stabiliisset, quas postea plurimi in Aula Parisiensi tum temporis versantes, ut nimium inquas exsibilaverant: Non ea recte improbari consilia, inquit Jovius, quibus cautus Imperator atque hostium expertus, magnis periculis occurrendum esse, & re sua fore duxerit.
units.tr: So that our most glorious Emperor could at last more readily check the licence of the Hungarian rebels, which until now has run unpunished, and crush their attempts from the root, he has also, in the most recent peace negotiations, most prudently striven to remove by every means the affairs of his rivals. And in these circumstances of our affairs and the turmoil of war, by which we are overwhelmed on every side, it is entirely fitting to bring forward here the judgment of Paolo Giovio, which he pronounced concerning Tremoille the Frenchman. In the time of Louis XII, King of the French, in the year 1513, at Dijon, Tremoille had more or less established some terms of peace with the Swiss on shifting sand. Many who were then at the Parisian court afterwards hissed these terms rather loudly. Giovio says: "Those plans are not rightly condemned by which a cautious commander, one experienced with enemies, judged that great dangers must be met and that his own interests would be served."

units.la: His itaque recte perpensis, quid quæso causæ est, cur non Alphonsi cognomento Sapientis, Arragoniæ Regis responsum, Dominico Firmiano Cardinali datum, cum ad Eum pro concilianda Italiæ Pace missus erat, paucis tantum mutatis verbis Invictissimo Cæsari nostro, sub præsenti Pacis nostræ susceptione ad suum quoque formemus animum & mores? Nunquam mihi
units.tr: Having therefore weighed these things rightly, what, I ask, is the reason why we should not likewise shape our own minds and conduct to the present acceptance of peace for our most invincible Emperor, by changing only a few words of the reply that Alfonso, surnamed the Wise, King of Aragon, gave to Cardinal Domenico Firmiano, when he was sent to him to bring about peace in Italy?

units.la: (sic respondebat Cardinali Firmiano Alphonsus) adeo secun-dæ res aut domi aut extra domum in bello fuerunt, quin si cum bello Pacem commutare licuerit, bello Pacem prætu-lerim: Nec vero nisi aut lacessitus, aut pro sociis ad hunc diem arma suscepi aut gessi. Nec me tam ratio ulla movit Imperii aut Regni augendi, quod Dei munere satis amplum esse atque opulentum scio, quam meæ ac Statuum Impe-rii quietis ac tranquillitatis; is semper finis consiliorum meorum fuit, ut absque injuria in Pace viverem: In bello Pacem, non in Pace bellum quærere soleo, &si quando no-bis hostis Pacem obtulit, nunquam eam aspernatus sum, nunquam rejeci, sed honestis conditionibus initis Pacem acceptavi, proque Amico imposterum habebo Regem Gal-liarum, & Regnorum meorum commercio ut olim perfrui patiar. Hoc posterius bellum Gallicanum jam neminem nescire arbitror, Batavorum sociorum & Amicorum causa, non ulla cupiditate mea à me suscEptum esse, quos cum ur-geri premique ab hostibus cernerem, non fuit æquitatis meæ, in tanto Status sui discrimine illos destituere. Non debuisset equidem, (ut cum Batavorum Pace loquar) Pa-cis nostræ ratio, quæ mea tantopere quoque referebat, me invito & inconsulto finiri, sed quæ acta sunt, redargui po-tius, quam emendari queunt: Ego per me stare nolim, quin hæc Pax atque armorum cessatio communis fiat: nolo consentientibus fœderatorum primariis ulterius de-esse, potissimum cum hanc ipsam Pacem, quemadmodum etiam Status Imperii agnoscunt, ad totius Imperii & Chri-stianitatis salutem & conservationem pertinere sciam: Sic majores mei, sic ego ab adolescentia institutus sum, ut tranquillitatem Imperii Romani omnibus rebus anteponam, nec Pontificis Maximi, cujus authoritatem, & fa-ctam [?]am interventionem plurimi facio, nec Principum Imperii & populorum nostrorum voluntati refragabor. Hæc, quæ ex ore Alphonsi Sapientis, Franciscus Tarapha, & Michael Ritius, ut & Vassæus nec non prolixius Lucius Marinæus Siculus annotata nobis publicârunt, ad rem præsentem omninò sunt servientia. Relinquan-tur itaque in medio, quæ nonnulli acri subtilique ingenio & judicio super has Pacis rationes percensebunt, aut infirmato judicio quidam alii malè dimetiri pote-runt: jam olim quoque hoc moris fuit curiosæ ho-minum frequentiæ, de qua re incidenter modo & quasi in transitu Tibi alicujus ingeniosi Itali Critticum quoddam examen & libram hic sisto, cui falsè admo-dum suo quoq; ævo Caroli IX. Galliarum Regis Pacis consilia subjecerat, quæ Anno CHRISTI 1568. in gratiam Principis Condæi & cæterorum Reforma-tæ Religioni addictorum suscepta erant: Ita autem ille in epistola quadam ad Amicum per risum & jocum subsannando scripserat:
units.tr: (Thus Alfonso answered Cardinal Firmiano.) "Never have my affairs gone so well, either at home or abroad in war, that I would not, if it were allowed to exchange war for peace, prefer peace to war. Nor have I ever taken up or waged arms until this day, unless I was provoked or fought for my allies. Nor has any reason so moved me to enlarge my empire or kingdom, which I know is large and wealthy enough by God's gift, as the quiet and tranquillity of my own realm and of my states. This has always been the aim of my plans: to live in peace without wrong. I am accustomed to seek war in order to have peace, not peace in order to have war. And if ever an enemy has offered us peace, I have never spurned it or rejected it, but on honourable terms I have accepted peace, and henceforth I will regard the King of the French as a friend and allow him to enjoy the commerce of my kingdoms as before. I think no one now is unaware that this later Gallic war was undertaken by me not from any desire of my own, but for the sake of my Dutch allies and friends. When I saw them pressed and oppressed by enemies, it was not consistent with my justice to abandon them in such great danger to their state. Indeed, as I speak of the Dutch peace, the reason of our peace, which concerned me so greatly too, ought not to have been concluded against my will and without my counsel. But what has been done can be challenged rather than corrected. I would not refuse to let this peace and this cessation of arms become common, provided that the chief allies agree. I do not wish to be lacking in anything further, especially since I know that the states of the Empire also acknowledge that this peace pertains to the safety and preservation of the whole Empire and of Christendom. My elders and I were brought up in this way from youth: to place the tranquillity of the Roman Empire before all things, and I will not oppose the authority and the intervention of the Supreme Pontiff, whose authority and intervention I greatly value, nor the will of the princes of the Empire and of our peoples." What Francesco Tarafa and Michele Ritio, as well as Vassaeus, and more fully Lucio Marineo Siculo, have published for us as noted from the mouth of Alfonso the Wise, is wholly suited to the present matter. Let us therefore leave in the middle what some will weigh with keen and subtle wit and judgment concerning these grounds of peace, or what others, with weakened judgment, may evaluate badly. It has long been the custom of curious gatherings of men, of which matter I now bring before you, in passing and as it were incidentally, a certain critical examination and balance by a certain ingenious Italian. He had falsely attached the counsels of peace to the time of Charles IX, King of the French, which were undertaken in the year of Christ 1568 for the sake of Prince Condé and the others devoted to the Reformed religion. He wrote this in a letter to a friend, mocking with jests and laughter, as follows:

units.la: La Pace è fatta: il Condè l' ha domandata: Il Maresciallo Momoransi l' ha manneggiata: la Marchese di Rottelino l' ha sollicitata: Il gia Cardinale Sciattiglione l' ha procurata: I Loreni l' hanno rivelata: Rocco - forte l' ha manifestata: la Spagna l' ha beffeggiata: Lansac l' ha spasseggiata: Il Cancelliere l' ha sigillata: L' Italia sene è maravigliata: Carnevalletto l' ha spronata: I Cattolici l' hanno disprezzata: I Parigini l' hanno dissimulata: La Francia ne è rovinata; i popoli l' hanno pagata: & Roma ne è scandalizzata:
units.tr: The peace is made. Condé asked for it. Marshal Montmorency managed it. The Marquise de Rottelin solicited it. The former Cardinal Châtillon procured it. The Lorrainers revealed it. Rocquefort made it manifest. Spain mocked it. Lansac strolled about it. The Chancellor sealed it. Italy has marvelled at it. Carnavalet spurred it on. The Catholics have despised it. The Parisians have dissembled it. France has been ruined by it; the peoples have paid for it; and Rome has been scandalised by it.

units.la: Vulgus hominum, & qui interiora Principum non penetrârunt, & tantum de medio sumpta norunt, semper leves visi & reperti sunt rerum publicarum & magnorum negotiorum Existimatores.
units.tr: The common crowd, and those who have not penetrated the inner counsels of princes and know only what is taken from the surface, have always seemed and proved to be shallow judges of public affairs and great undertakings.

units.la: Sunt enim Reges & rerumpublicarum Ministri in alia longe spectabiliori prae caeteris statione collocati, tanquam in specula & liberali custodia, ut invigilent communibus bonis, & cum aliqua vis major ingruit, eam diligere partem debent, ad quam eos convertit inclinatio temporum, ratio concordiae, salus populi, quam semper pro suprema lege & optimo more censeri oportet. Haec Dominicus Baudius, cùm de induciis Belgicis ageretur, sapienter aliquando Batavis suis, denen Herren Staaten suggessit.
units.tr: For kings and the ministers of commonwealths are placed in a far more conspicuous station than others, as on a watchtower and under liberal guard, so that they may watch over the common goods; and when some greater force bears down, they ought to choose that side to which the inclination of the times, the reason of concord and the safety of the people turn them, which must always be counted as the supreme law and the best custom. Thus Dominicus Baudius, when the Belgian truces were under discussion, once wisely suggested to his Dutch countrymen, to the Lords States.

units.la: Manebit igitur sacratissimo Austriaco nostro sua Pacis laurus, illæsa brumis, intacta fulminibus, solibus nullis obnoxia, mori nescia, nisi inter triumphantes comas. Sed cùm con-sultius sit, plura hodie tacere, quàm eloqui, concludam orationem meam, id solum ro-gans, ut legens illam, non universitati ejus at-tendas, verum etiam particulari sensui. Vale & Amico Veteri veterem offer animum, & officia à me expecta perpetuò prompta:
units.tr: Therefore the laurel of peace will remain for our most sacred Austrian, unharmed by frosts, untouched by thunderbolts, subject to no suns, unable to die, except among triumphant hair. But since it is more prudent today to keep many things silent than to speak them, I will conclude my oration, asking only this: that in reading it you attend not to its whole sense, but also to its particular meaning. Farewell, and offer your old friend your old spirit, and expect from me services always ready.

units.la: Iterum Vale.
units.tr: Farewell again.
